summary: Part VII completes the Mount Ebott Survey Expedition. Picking up immediately after Papyrus's dusting in the false meadow, Sans experiences a fleeting memory of drinking tea with King Asgore before snapping back to freeze time and brutally execute Flowey in a burst of violent blue magic. The Agent recovers the survey machine—discovering it recorded the entire fight—and attempts to wear it as a backpack before the straps fail. Guided by Sans through the Underground's cave loop, the group reaches New Home Castle, where the Agent uses official Iron Legion documents signed by Commissar Vexis to bluff past the royal guards. In the throne room, King Asgore and Queen Toriel explain the Barrier's delicate balance and agree to grant localized transport to the surface under a binding Oath of Secrecy.

sections.name: I. The Immediate Aftermath — How to Kill a Flower
sections.overview:
The white dust from Papyrus's body hung suspended in the calm air of the false meadow for a single heartbeat before dispersing into the grass. His dark coat lay flat on the multi-colored tile grid. The blue gravity cage had shattered into glowing shards that faded into nothingness. Sans stood motionless in the center of the field, his hands half-raised, his eye sockets pitch black and completely devoid of white lights.

The Agent turned his gaze toward Dracule Mihawk, his boots stepping over a cold brass tile. He gave a firm, singular nod.

**"We need to kill Flowey,"** the Agent said.

Mihawk did not hesitate. His golden eye locked onto the distant patch of loam where the yellow petals had submerged into the earth. With a single, fluid motion, the Warlord drew Yoru from his back sheath. The massive black blade caught the artificial sunlight, casting a sharp shadow across the soil.

**"Agreed,"** Mihawk said coldly, taking a measured step forward.

**"How do we kill a flower?"** the Agent asked, adjusting his posture and scanning the perimeter for vine movement.

Mihawk tilted his head slightly, assessing the target with dispassionate tactical logic.

**"Burn it,"** Mihawk replied plainly, his fingers adjusting on Yoru's hilt. **"Fire is effective against plants."**

Sans remained motionless beside them, his shoulders hunched under his blue hoodie, his breath coming out slow and shallow as the dust settled on his boots.

*WAH! Waluigi agrees completely with this tactical assessment! When a garden specimen murders a municipal officer from behind during an emotional admission, you do not prune it! You do not give it plant food or put it in a decorative ceramic pot! You fetch a torch and incinerate the entire flowerbed until there is nothing left but carbon! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: Observe that Dracule Mihawk does not attempt to categorize Flowey as a duelist or a combatant of honor. He categorizes him as agricultural pestilence. In military operations, treating an opportunistic wildcard as a formal opponent is a fatal error. Mihawk's immediate recommendation of fire reflects proper elemental counter-measures against root-based entities. WAH.

sections.name: II. The Midnight Tea — Sans's Memory of Asgore
sections.overview:
Before Mihawk could strike his blade into the soil, the air around Sans warped violently. The fake meadow, the bright sky, and the color-tile grid dissolved for a brief, suspended moment as reality folded inward, drawing Sans into the quiet warmth of a distant memory.

It was night inside the royal castle at New Home. Outside the leaded glass windows, the Underground was dark and still. Sans sat at a heavy oak table while King Asgore walked slowly across the stone floor, carrying a steaming clay teapot.

**"The tea is ready!"** Asgore announced pleasantly, pouring a golden liquid into two cups.

Sans took the cup, blowing softly on the steam before taking a careful sip. **"Thank you, Asgore. It smells lovely... As good as always."**

Asgore smiled across the table, his large paws wrapped around his teacup. **"I really am thankful that you decided to come over, Sans. I wasn't sure I'd ever have outside visitors again, but... It's been too long since I've had company. The castle feels... quieter than it used to. I hope you enjoy the tea, it's an old recipe of mine."**

**"It's excellent as always,"** Sans replied, leaning back in his wooden chair. **"It's been a rough few months lately. I needed an evening like this."**

**"Ho ho ho! I'm so glad you like it!"** Asgore chuckled softly.

Sans smirked, a hint of genuine warmth returning to his eye sockets. **"You never stop being so positive and kind, do you? You could never serve a bad cup of tea, Asgore. You'd need to lose your hands before that happened."**

Asgore's expression turned earnest as he set his cup down. **"I would like to catch up on your lives, if you will. Tell me, what do you do for an occupation? I am very curious to know what goes on outside these caverns."**

Sans folded his hands over his stomach. **"Well, I work as a sentry. It's not a particularly exciting job, but... it keeps me busy. You know the usual. I keep an eye out for humans, patrol the Snowdin woods, and... sleep on the job."**

Asgore paused, his brow furrowing gently. **"What do you think about the whole catching humans thing?"**

Sans exhaled slowly, looking down into his golden tea. **"Honestly? I don't agree with it. I've never caught a human. Never wanted to."**

Asgore gazed at him with quiet, paternal trust. **"I understand it's difficult to find the will to do what we must. But from what I can tell, you are an honest young man. I believe when the time comes you will do the right thing. So tell me... what keeps you going?"**

Sans tapped his knuckles softly against the clay cup. **"Honestly? My brother. Papyrus... he keeps me going. I wanna make him proud, you know? He believes in being strong and noble, so I try to match that energy for him. And then there are little things too — like my friends in Snowdin. Grillby's diner..."**

**"There is nothing wrong in finding solace in others,"** Asgore said softly. **"I assure you if we had more people like you and your brother we will have a peaceful future someday. Promise me this will you, Sans? Never give up this dream."**

Sans looked past Asgore at the peaceful darkness outside the glass. **"Yeah... I do. More than anything, I want peace. I want everyone I care about to be happy and safe... A world where everyone can just... live without fighting. Without fear."**

*WAH! The quiet tea-table summit! A depressed goat king and a sentry who refuses to do his job sitting in a castle drinking herbal tea at midnight! This memory explains everything about Sans! He spent four years sleeping at his guard post in Snowdin not because he was lazy, but because he promised King Asgore he would choose peace over human-hunting! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: This memory is the exact structural anchor that held Sans together. His refusal to capture humans was not insubordination; it was compliance with a personal oath made to Asgore. When Flowey killed Papyrus, he did not merely murder a brother — he severed the exact reason Sans maintained his peaceful restraint. WAH.

sections.name: III. The Freeze and the Eruption — Sans Executes Flowey
sections.overview:
The memory snapped shut like a heavy book. Sans blinked, his eyelights snapping back into the present meadow where Flowey's golden head had just re-emerged from the dirt to mock them.

Time froze. A sharp, loud *CLICK* echoed through the clearing as the entire world shifted into monochrome grayscale. Sans vanished from where he stood and materialized instantaneously directly beside Flowey. His eye sockets were pitch black.

**"Look at me,"** Sans whispered. His voice was lower than death itself. **"You hurt Papyrus."**

Flowey's petals trembled in sudden, frantic panic. **"YOU DAMN BRAT!"** the flower shrieks, whipping his vines forward. **"YOU THINK A BATTLE CAN SAVE YOU!"**

A catastrophic spell erupted from Sans in a blinding burst of violent blue magic. The surge struck Flowey dead-on, scorching his petals and blasting him across the dirt in a shower of sparks.

Flowey hit the ground hard, but Sans was already standing over him. Sans grabbed Flowey by the central stem and slammed him brutally into the earth, creating a jagged crater in the soil.

**"COME ON!"** Sans roared, his jaw set as brilliant blue fire flared wildly from his left socket. **"WHERE'S THAT SPIRIT NOW!?!"** He slammed the flower down again—*BAM!* **"ANSWER ME! You don't get to hide! Why did you do it?! What was the point of hurting my brother!? ANSWER ME RIGHT NOW!"**

He pounded the flower into the dirt three more times until the stem broke and the petals disintegrated into black ash.

Time snapped back into motion with a loud pop. Color flooded back into the meadow. Sans lowered his shaking hands, staring down at the crushed ash in the crater.

The Agent stepped forward, staring at the ruined soil. **"Sans... he's dead. The flower is dead, you killed it."**

Sans exhaled slowly, his eyelights returning as dim white pinpricks. **"Guess I did,"** he muttered quietly. **"He deserved it."**

*WAH! Time-stop beatdowns! Never make a short skeleton angry in front of a flower! Sans went from zero magical reserve to a localized apocalyptic execution in three-tenths of a second! Flowey learned the hard way that 'where is that spirit now' is not a rhetorical question! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: Notice that Sans did not use a complex puzzle, a bone storm, or a platform trap. He used absolute proximity and raw kinetic magic. When the limits of restraint are removed, Sans's combat efficiency is staggering. Flowey was given no opportunity to burrow, reset, or summon vines. WAH.

sections.name: IV. The Survey Machine Record — Ecological Miscalibration
sections.overview:
With Flowey eliminated, the clearing grew silent. The Agent walked over to the Iron Legion survey machine resting on the grass, its heavy brass housing humming softly as data tray light flickered.

The monitor screen displayed scrolling lines of text. The Agent stared at the monitor in utter disbelief—the machine had recorded the entire battle in meticulous detail. Timestamped movement vectors, magical energy spikes, the gravity cage collapse, and even Sans's final time-stop execution were fully logged alongside soil acidity and humidity readings.

Mihawk stepped alongside him, crossing his arms as he examined the glowing display. **"Hm. That thing picked up everything."**

**"It's meant for ecological surveys,"** the Agent said, frowning at the screen. **"How did it record combat data?"**

Mihawk leaned in closer, his golden eye taking in the scrolling columns. **"This data is messy. Half ecological readings, half combat logs. Soil samples and energy spikes... The device has been broken, repaired, and re-patched too many times to function properly. It picked up the magic by accident."**

The Agent nodded, reaching down to unbuckle the heavy leather harness. **"Whatever. I'm re-attaching the survey device and grabbing the straps to make a makeshift backpack. It's heavy, but we won't lose it this way — not again."**

He hoisted the bulky 80-pound brass unit onto his back, pulling the leather straps tight across his chest plate. He took two steps before the leather groaned under the strain. The makeshift harness snapped with a loud crack, and the survey device slid violently down his legs, clunking heavily against the dirt with a thud that shook the grass.

The Agent stared down at the dropped machine, rubbing his shoulder. **"It will not hold."**

Mihawk exhaled dryly through his nose. **"Told you."**

*WAH! Repurposed technology! An ecological survey device that accidentally logged a murder and a time-stop assault because its sensors could not tell the difference between a root sample and a Gaster Blaster! Iron Legion engineering at its finest! And strap failure! Waluigi has told Wario a hundred times that you cannot wear a brass boiler as a rucksack! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: The Agent's attempt to convert a stationary survey apparatus into a backpack using worn leather straps is a classic field error. Scientific instruments weighing eighty pounds require standardized transport carts or anti-gravity cradles. Attempting to wear them as luggage results in broken straps and bruised ankles. WAH.

sections.name: V. Egress Doctrine — The Law of the Barrier
sections.overview:
Leaving the dropped machine on the grass for a moment, the Agent looked toward Sans. **"We just have to get out of here. Asgore and the Queen know how to, right?"**

Sans scanned the quiet meadow, his posture weary. **"We should go... before anything else happens. I think we need to find an exit from this place, somewhere that will take us back to New Home. Maybe the queen or Asgore can help. I don't know the exact way from here, though."**

The Agent raised an eyebrow. **"The Queen... you call her that a lot, but other people say Toriel. Why is that? Is her title not that big?"**

Sans's expression turned stern. **"To me, she's the queen. Toriel is her name, yeah. But she's also the queen of monsters. She deserves to be called by her title. She's one of the only people I've met who is worthy of respect. So to me, she's the queen. Nothing less."**

The Agent nodded, then glanced around. **"Without a map... I guess we can discuss what to do if the Friendship comes back with Gaster and his pirates."**

Mihawk glanced over curiously. **"You're expecting the Friendship to return?"**

**"Yes, why wouldn't I?"** the Agent replied.

Mihawk folded his arms. **"Gaster's crew is unpredictable. They come and go as they please. If they do come back, we'll see what their intentions are before assuming anything helpful will happen."**

The Agent turned back to Sans. **"Also, Asgore and the Queen... Sans, you said they won't just let us out. Why? Why is leaving the Underground a different process than just leaving the Old World where I live?"**

Sans rubbed his skull thoughtfully. **"Leaving the Underground isn't like leaving any random place in your world. There are rules down here. Laws. Barriers. A long time ago... a powerful human wizard put all of us here. He was trying to keep humans from leaving, but he kept us monsters trapped as well. The only way to leave... is for a human and monster to work together."**

**"So can you even leave when we try to exit?"** the Agent asked.

**"Technically? Yeah,"** Sans explained. **"The wards don't stop us from exiting the Underground itself. But once we step out of here... we can't come back in easily. And if something happens on the surface..."**

**"And the humans won the war?"**

**"Yeah,"** Sans said softly. **"The humans won. They drove us underground and sealed us away permanently. To break the barrier for good... it takes massive effort. Both humans and monsters working together willingly."**

*WAH! Dimensional boundary laws! The barrier was built by an ancient human wizard who wanted to lock monsters away, but he built the lock so poorly that people can leave but cannot get back in! Typical human wizard work — grand concept, terrible administrative execution! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: Notice the asymmetrical nature of the magical barrier. Individual egress is permitted under specific energy thresholds, but re-entry is blocked. This design prevents surface forces from launching counter-invasions while forcing exiting individuals into permanent exile. WAH.

sections.name: VI. The Cave Loop — Teleportation Under Whispers
sections.overview:
Sans took a deep breath, steeling himself. **"Alright. Let me take the lead."**

He raised a hand, his eye sockets flashing with a brief spark of blue light. The air around them folded inward, and the false meadow dissolved into dark, echoing stone corridors.

They began walking briskly through the dimly lit tunnels. The Agent checked his wrist watch, tapping the glass face. **"Huh. We've been walking for about twenty minutes now."**

He looked around, noticing the grand architectural spires of New Home Castle looming directly ahead through the gloom. **"So you teleported us closer to the king. I thought that was a random field, but you seemed to know where to go."**

Sans shrugged casually. **"Yeah... I knew where to go. The castle isn't exactly hard to find if you're familiar with the Underground. The Underground loops like a cave system — everything connects eventually if you walk far enough. There aren't really 'lost' places down here... just ones that are harder to get to. And this place? It's one of the major points on that loop."**

The Agent slowed his pace slightly, stepping alongside Mihawk. He leaned in and whispered softly: **"That was way too fast, don't you think? No interruptions... suddenly we're in the tunnels, then we're here that fast near the capital."**

Mihawk kept his gaze fixed ahead, his voice low and unbothered. **"Teleportation is fast... yes. But not unusual for monsters with magic. The capital isn't far from here anyway. It's normal to..."**

He cut himself off as three heavily armored royal guards stepped out from the shadows near the castle gates.

*WAH! Spatial shortcuts! You think you are walking three miles through damp granite, but a skeleton blinks his eye sockets and suddenly you are standing in the king's front yard! Spatial efficiency or lazy map design? Waluigi says both! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: The Underground's geography operates on closed topology. Major hubs (Snowdin, Hotland, New Home) connect via compressed spatial corridors. Sans's ability to navigate these shortcuts allows the team to bypass days of transit in twenty minutes. WAH.

sections.name: VII. The Gate Guard Bluff — The Commissar Vexis Documents
sections.overview:
The royal guards lowered their halberds, blocking the arched entrance to the courtyard. **"Halt!"** the lead guard commanded sharply. **"State your business!"**

The guards narrowed their eyes, hands resting firmly on their sword hilts. **"You there! Identify yourselves and state why you're approaching the castle!"**

Sans hesitated for a second too long, unsure how to frame their arrival. The lead guard stepped forward, his voice dripping with warning. **"Last chance. Answer!"**

The Agent nudged Sans aside, stepping forward with crisp military posture. He puffed out his chest and spoke in a clear, practiced cadence: **"We are the Iron Legion Commissar Royal Expedition Unit, codename Lone Snake, color Green. Primary purpose: classified due to being currently active. Secondary purpose: survey of unfamiliar area."**

The guards blinked, utterly taken aback by the barrage of formal military terminology. **"Iron Legion...? Commissar?"** the lead guard muttered, exchanging bewildered looks with his men. **"We weren't informed of any royal expedition unit arriving today. Do you have proof of your rank and mission parameters?"**

**"Yes,"** the Agent replied smoothly. **"I have papers issued by Commissar Vexis."**

He reached into his inner coat pocket and produced an official folder stamped with gold foil and sealed with heavy red wax, handing it to the lead guard.

The guards crowded around, inspecting the documents carefully. **"Hmph. These look legitimate enough..."** the lead guard admitted begrudgingly, scrutinizing the official seal and Commissar Vexis's signature. **"Though we were never issued orders regarding a commissar... Very well. You may enter... for now."**

As they passed through the gates, Sans mumbled quietly with a smirk: **"Guess those documents actually worked after all. We got lucky there. Good on you for getting all that military jargon down."**

**"Guess they're slow on the uptake, the guards,"** the Agent chuckled.

*WAH! Bureaucratic intimidation! Nothing confuses a checkpoint guard faster than a man in a green coat reading out sixteen syllables of fake classification numbers! Waluigi uses this exact trick when entering VIP lounges at kart races! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: Notice how easily the guards yielded when presented with wax-sealed paperwork signed by Commissar Vexis. Security personnel in formal hierarchies are trained to fear administrative reprimand more than unauthorized entry. A gold foil seal is effectively an invisible key. WAH.

sections.name: VIII. The Throne Room Audience — King Asgore and Queen Toriel
sections.overview:
The grand wooden doors of the castle creaked open, revealing a vast throne room lit by flickering chandeliers and carpeted in golden buttercups. At the far end sat King Asgore upon his massive stone throne, his red cape draped over his shoulders and his trident resting beside his seat. Standing near him as royal advisor was Queen Toriel, her hands folded neatly in her white robes.

Asgore looked up slowly as the group entered, his voice booming through the hall. **"Who approaches my court? I don't recall being informed of an official military expedition passing through the Underground... nor a royal escort either. I'm not used to unexpected guests in my home, especially armed ones."**

The Agent stepped forward, lowering his hands. **"Oh no, we mean this place no harm. We are seeking an exit."**

Asgore's expression shifted into a contemplative frown. **"An exit...?"**

Toriel stepped forward gently, her golden eyes filled with quiet concern. **"And what exactly do you mean by 'seeking an exit,' child? Do you wish to leave permanently?"**

**"Yes, we wish to go to the surface,"** the Agent affirmed.

Asgore leaned back on his throne, steepling his large claws. **"I see... And you believe there is an exit that can be opened? That it hasn't been sealed beyond return?"**

**"No, no,"** the Agent clarified, gesturing to Sans. **"Our skeleton friend here told us you would be able to help see us out."**

Asgore scrutinized Sans. **"He is the one who suggested you seek me out for assistance? And you believe I have the power to simply... open a path for you? Just like that? The logistics of opening a path to the surface are not simple."**

Sans stepped forward, dropping his casual demeanor entirely. **"We're aware the barrier isn't easy to undo... but if anyone could do it, you could, right?"**

*WAH! Royal court manners! Entering a throne room with a giant sword and a broken survey machine is usually a recipe for getting executed, but King Asgore is so polite he offers tea before asking why you are standing on his rug! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: The audience in the throne room transitions the expedition from tactical survival to high diplomacy. Asgore and Toriel receive the group not as invaders, but as petitioning travelers seeking egress. WAH.

sections.name: IX. Barrier Logistics — Localized Transport vs Mass Destruction
sections.overview:
Asgore stroked his golden beard thoughtfully, his eyes heavy with ancient responsibility. **"Breaking through centuries of magical barriers is no small task... It would require immense power and precision."**

Toriel nodded in agreement. **"If we attempt this... it must be done carefully. The last thing we need is for the barrier to collapse entirely or cause catastrophic damage."**

The Agent frowned. **"The last thing you want is for it to collapse...? Why wouldn't you want to destroy it?"**

Asgore explained in measured tones. **"Destroying it outright would risk destabilizing the Underground entirely. The magic that keeps us here isn't just a prison — it's also what maintains our world as we know it. Think of it this way: if we tear down the barrier completely without care, the magic sustaining our world isn't infinite. It's balanced. Without careful control... everything could collapse inward like a dying star."**

Toriel added gently: **"And even worse — imagine if dangerous creatures or surface forces got through before proper precautions were taken! The surface wouldn't be safe either!"**

The Agent considered this before offering an alternative: **"Then fine. Can we use a localized transport where we just send two people out?"**

Asgore looked thoughtful. **"Yes... a localized transport might be an option. It would require tremendous power, but it could allow a few to pass through more safely."**

Toriel stepped forward, her expression turning serious. **"However... there is one other factor to consider. If we do this... you must understand that it's possible you may never return. Are you prepared for such a life?"**

The Agent met her gaze firmly. **"Yes. I feel like I have gained what I wanted to here."**

*WAH! Localized portal physics! Instead of tearing down the whole wall and letting the roof collapse, you cut a small envelope-sized hole in reality and push two men through! Precision magic over raw force every time! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: Asgore's refusal to destroy the Barrier outright is rooted in ecological physics. The Barrier regulates the Underground's internal magic balance. A localized transport bypasses the barrier without destroying its structural load. WAH.

sections.name: X. The Oath of Secrecy — The Final Terms
sections.overview:
Asgore and Toriel exchanged a brief, meaningful look, coming to a silent agreement.

**"Very well then,"** Asgore said, his deep voice carrying finality. **"We are willing to attempt the transport. I will prepare the necessary spellwork. However..."**

Toriel stepped forward, her expression stern yet protective. **"We must ask one condition of you before we continue."**

**"What is it?"** the Agent asked.

Asgore folded his hands together over his chest. **"Before we proceed... you must swear an oath. An oath of secrecy regarding the Underground and its people."**

Toriel emphasized every word: **"You cannot reveal our world to humans on the surface. Not fully, not carelessly. The safety of monsters depends on this barrier remaining intact in everyone's minds as a myth — not a reality they can exploit."**

The Agent, Mihawk, and Sans stood together before the throne. The weight of the vow settled heavily in the air. The expedition had achieved its objective, but the price of egress was absolute silence.

*WAH! The Non-Disclosure Agreement of Mount Ebott! A solemn vow made to a goat king and a queen that keeps seven hundred thousand underground monsters off surface television! Waluigi approves of non-disclosure agreements, especially when they prevent tax auditors from finding hidden gold reserves! WAH.*
sections.waluigi_note: The Oath of Secrecy serves as the final diplomatic barrier. It ensures that while individuals may exit, the Underground remains protected by mythological obscurity. WAH.

aftermath:
## Aftermath & Operational Standing

**1. Operational Result:** The Mount Ebott Survey Expedition successfully reached the political center of the Underground at New Home Castle. The primary objective—locating an egress route to the surface—was negotiated directly with King Asgore and Queen Toriel.

**2. Casualty & Personnel Status:** Papyrus was assassinated in Part VI. Flowey was subsequently executed by Sans in a time-stop magic eruption. Sans remains mentally exhausted but operational. Dracule Mihawk and the Legionary Agent sustained minor graze injuries.

**3. Materiel & Intelligence:** The Iron Legion survey machine was recovered, containing complete combat logs and barrier energy signatures despite its ecological miscalibration. Official Iron Legion documentation issued by Commissar Vexis proved 100% effective in bypassing municipal security checkpoints.

**4. Diplomatic Agreement:** Egress will be executed via localized transport spellcraft, subject to a binding Oath of Secrecy regarding the Underground's existence.
waluigiAssessment:
## Waluigi's Assessment & Editorial Verdict

**1. The Egress Protocol — A Masterclass in Localized Transport.** Waluigi commends King Asgore and Queen Toriel for rejecting the total destruction of the Barrier. Destroying a load-bearing dimensional seal to move two men is like blowing up a bridge to cross a puddle. Localized transport is clean, efficient, and keeps the roof where it belongs. WAH.

**2. The Vexis Credentials — Administrative Victory.** The Agent's use of Commissar Vexis's papers proves Waluigi's long-standing thesis: guards at official gates do not read documents to verify truth; they read documents to relieve themselves of responsibility. A gold seal and a commissar's name will get you into almost any room in the multiverse. WAH.

**3. The Execution of Flowey — Functional Retribution.** Flowey's elimination by Sans in a localized time-stop was necessary for operational security. Allowing a hostile entity with cross-dimensional boundary data to remain mobile would have compromised both the Underground and surface operations. WAH.

**4. The Oath of Secrecy — Legal Recommendation.** Waluigi advises all readers to respect the Oath of Secrecy. Not because of royal authority, but because if humans on the surface discover seven hundred thousand monsters living under a mountain, they will immediately try to tax them. WAH.

**Final Recommendation:** Approve the Part VII filing. Close the Mount Ebott Survey dossier. File the Vexis documents in the Iron Legion archives under Class 1 Clearance. WAH!

*"All recordings are now inactive."* — the last sentence on the Mount Ebott logger before High Command turned the archive off.

The final Mount Ebott log begins with a promise that the surface will not learn too much and ends with High Command making sure the archive cannot learn any more. That is the shape of the whole file: every institution in the room wants control over what may be known. Asgore and Toriel want monsterkind protected by silence. The Iron Legion wants the survey machine and all the data it secretly gathered. The Gamma Agent wants one hour a month to call home. Mihawk wants to leave with his dignity intact and without being made a prisoner for standing near a classified mission. Jamesly wants the Agent contained before talent becomes scandal. Daniel wants a discipline hearing until the Deadman's Stamp turns discipline into a leak investigation. High Command wants the final conversation off the public record.

The document therefore cannot be filed as a simple extraction. The extraction succeeds in the first half. The problem is what extraction *means* after the machine reaches Legion hands. A person can swear silence. A device cannot feel bound by an oath it was never told about. By the time the Gamma Agent understands that the survey machine has logged conversations, battles, energy levels, and monster technology, the Underground's secrecy has already been converted into a case file.

Waluigi files the final log as the moment the Mount Ebott survey stops being an expedition and becomes an argument about custody of knowledge. The party got out. The machine got out. The truth got out in a box. Then High Command closed the box on the archive itself.

The final log is also personal in ways its institutions try to sand flat. The Agent's request for outside communication is not merely a reward request; it is a person asking whether successful service buys the right to hear family again. Mihawk's quiet talk about an unnamed island is not merely biography; it is the sound of a man who has crossed a sealed world and still does not know where to stand next. Even the officer's fear matters. She is not only a source of information. She is a person learning that the manual she trusted was not the real manual. Waluigi files these things because an archive that records only protocols has already surrendered to the people who write protocols.

sections.name: The Oath That Made the Exit Legal
sections.overview:
Asgore did not treat the departure as a favor. He treated it as a risk with witnesses attached. His voice was steady because a king is expected to sound steady when saying dangerous things in a room that needs him steady. The Underground had endured for generations by remaining half rumor, half story, the kind of place the surface could dismiss as legend until curiosity became too expensive. If humans learned monsters were real, the old injuries could become fresh policy. Toriel made the same point with fewer ornaments and more finality: the oath was non-negotiable. Silence on what was seen. Silence on how they left. Silence not merely as etiquette but as survival.

The room waited for the answers. Sans swore first, quiet and firm, not because he had no doubts but because betrayal of monsterkind had no use to him after everything already lost. Mihawk answered in the way Mihawk answers many things: a single slow nod, arms crossed, loyalty reduced to the smallest motion that still counts. The Gamma Agent watched the others and the survey machine both. The oath entered the file as [[prop:prop_ebott_secrecy_oath|a contract made out loud]], but the machine sitting nearby was already becoming a second witness.

That tension is the entire seed of the final log. The Underground believed it was negotiating with people. It was. It was also negotiating in the presence of an object with broader memory than its operator understood. The Agent did not yet know that; ignorance is not malice. But ignorance does not delete a recording. Waluigi notes the oath as legally serious, morally serious, and structurally doomed the moment the wrong device crossed the threshold.

Then Asgore rose and the throne room moved from politics to mechanism. Toriel went to gather what was needed. The air changed. The farewell had become a procedure.
sections.waluigi_note: An oath before a machine is how serious people make a door. Waluigi prefers doors with hinges, but monarchs love ceremony. WAH.

sections.name: Gaster's Blaster Was a Door, Not a Gun
sections.overview:
The scientist entered like a man rolling in a holiday. Wing Gaster was squat, bright-eyed behind thick glasses, and wrapped in an apron that made the machine look less like an execution device and more like something a very excited baker had overbuilt. Blue lights pulsed along the frame. The apparatus hummed into the marble. Asgore watched with royal fatigue. Toriel returned solemnly, less interested in the scientist's pride than in the cost of success.

Gaster introduced himself as Royal Scientist and announced the CORE as his greatest creation. He was not simply preparing a transport; he was narrating the day he believed history would remember him for. The Agent whispered to Mihawk that the name sounded familiar. Mihawk considered the pirate Gaster from earlier in the expedition, measured the face, the manner, and the aura, and refused to overstate the resemblance. The scientist was cheerful, not cold. Names, however, are not common, and Mount Ebott had already taught the file that names can echo across impossible places without asking permission.

The platform lit. Mihawk stepped up first. Then the Gaster Blaster appeared beside Gaster and charged. In any sane room, a skull-shaped cannon materializing beside a scientist would end the conversation. Here, Gaster announced it as an invention: a stabilized dimensional projector for long-range transport. The blaster's beam struck the platform, swallowed Mihawk in light, and left the room with the terrible residue of dust-like shimmer.

The Agent checked the dust because under Mount Ebott dust has a history and a body count. Asgore said Mihawk was not dead. Toriel said he was simply elsewhere. Sans briefly called that elsewhere another world; the Agent corrected him. The surface was not another dimension. Gaster confirmed it: local-dimensional displacement within the same world's plane. This correction matters more than it first sounds. The Underground did not open a multiversal gate. It authorized a route to the surface. A gun-shaped door is still a door, and the oath applied to where it led.
sections.waluigi_note: The machine uses a skull cannon to do transportation. This is why scientists should be supervised by accountants and frightened gardeners.

sections.name: Koffin-K Arrived Too Late to Explain the Emergency
sections.overview:
The Agent stepped onto the platform after Mihawk. The room had already seen the procedure work once, which made it more frightening rather than less. The first transport proved the machine could take someone. It did not prove what else it could interrupt, attract, or leave behind. Gaster's hands moved quickly over the controls. The core brightened, throwing blue across Asgore's face. Toriel folded her hands. Sans received one look from the Agent, and whatever that look asked was never answered.

Gaster began the count. Three. Two. Then the door burst open hard enough to make the room forget the number after two. Koffin-K stood in the threshold with urgency stripped of theatre. He was not posing, boasting, or decorating his entrance with villain style. He shouted for them to wait. He said they could not send the Agent through yet. He said there was an emergency.

That is all the archive has. Gaster froze mid-countdown and asked what emergency. Asgore straightened. The room recognized the interruption as serious because Koffin-K had abandoned the performance by which everyone normally identified him. But the machine did not wait for the archive to receive a better sentence. The light took the Agent before the emergency could be named.

This is an unresolved lead, not a dramatic flourish. Koffin-K might have discovered a threat behind them, a consequence of Papyrus and Flowey, a failure in the transport, a political reversal, or something ridiculous delivered with perfect bad timing. The file cannot say. The investigation therefore keeps the warning as warning. Waluigi refuses to invent the missing content simply because the story wants a cleaner hinge. Sometimes the door opens, someone shouts, and history becomes light before the verb arrives.
sections.waluigi_note: A warning that arrives one syllable late is still evidence. It is also infuriating. File the interruption; do not invent the contents.

sections.name: The Machine Was Never Only Ecological
sections.overview:
The surface smelled like grass. That should have been the emotional center of the file: sky above, air moving naturally, birds in the distance, Mihawk already standing there and answering the Agent's question with a plain yes. They had done it. They had left the Underground without breaking the Barrier, without killing the King, without reducing the oath to a trick. For one breath, the mission could pretend to be complete.

Then the helicopter spotlight found them.

The Legion arrived cheerful and professional. The soldiers treated the extraction as a success because, from their side, it was. Target acquired. Data recovered. Assets alive. The Agent handed over the survey machine and the data packet. The receiving soldier secured them in a reinforced case and said the intelligence would change everything. That sentence is either praise or indictment depending on which side of the oath one is standing.

Only after the handoff did the machine's true scope become explicit. The Agent asked whether it had been meant to log battles, conversations, and other material. He had thought it was for ecological data. The soldier answered with a laugh: ecology, yes, but also conversations, battle readings, energy levels, monster tech scans. The receipt now filed as [[prop:prop_ebott_data_handover_receipt|the handover ledger]] confirms the mismatch. The Agent was not merely delivering what he believed he collected. He was delivering what the Legion's equipment had collected through him.

This does not make the Agent a liar. It makes him an instrument who was not told the instrument had another blade folded inside it. That is worse for the oath in a different way. Asgore and Toriel extracted a promise from people who could choose. The machine had already chosen nothing and remembered everything. Waluigi files this as the moment the survey mission's stated purpose collapses under its own hardware.
sections.waluigi_note: If your ecological scanner records conversations, it is not an ecological scanner. It is a clerk with a battery. WAH.

sections.name: The Embassy Sorted People Into Uses
sections.overview:
The embassy did not simply receive the expedition. It sorted it. The rooftop took the helicopter. The intake desk took the machine. The first briefing room took the Agent. The secondary chamber took Mihawk. Every hallway performed a small act of classification: asset, witness, non-Legion exposure, data carrier, command problem. The building's high-tech cleanliness is therefore not background decoration. It is the visual language of a place that wants all dirt converted into files before anyone can call it dirt.

The Agent enters with a machine and leaves the first room with a privilege. Mihawk enters with a sword and leaves with a surveillance problem attached. Neither outcome is random. The embassy knows how to reward a useful operator and how to make a polite cage for a useful witness. It does both without raising its voice. That is why the location gets its own record: not because the walls are interesting, but because the walls are part of the procedure.

Waluigi notes that the embassy's mirrored glass is almost too honest. A mirror lets one side watch while the other side sees only itself. That is exactly how the Legion uses debriefing here. The Agent thinks he is explaining the mission; the embassy is measuring the operator. Mihawk thinks he is answering whether he collected data; the embassy is deciding how much memory a free man is allowed to carry. The rooms are not passive. They are tools.
sections.waluigi_note: A building that separates witnesses before anyone asks is not a building. It is a questionnaire with elevators.

sections.name: The Flight That Refused Geography
sections.overview:
The High Command summons should have produced a long flight: borders, airspace clearances, fuel, time to think, time for the Agent to regret how much he had said to the embassy officer. The Agent even complains that the trip will cross a lot of borders for something that could have been handled by video call. The pilot answers with clearance. Then the world stops behaving like clearance is the hard part.

The helicopter reaches High Command too quickly. The Agent notices. He had expected days and gets arrival. He expected Mushroom Kingdom borders and gets a spire. The pilot does not explain. No guard stops him. The elevator rises at a speed that makes height feel like a rumor. By the time the chamber opens, the file has quietly changed genres again: this is no longer only a military chain of command. It is infrastructure that can cheat distance.

That matters because the Mount Ebott survey began as a geography problem. A mountain, a hole, a route down, a route out. The final movement is the opposite. High Command demonstrates that it can make distance collapse when it wants a Gamma Agent in a room. This turns the summons into more than orders. It is a display of reach. The Agent is not merely being called somewhere; he is being shown that 'somewhere' is negotiable for the people doing the calling.
sections.waluigi_note: When a helicopter trip skips the map, the map is either wrong or outranked. Waluigi dislikes both options.

sections.name: One Hour a Month, Monitored
sections.overview:
The embassy converted success into procedure. The building itself seemed designed to make the Agent's return feel less like rescue and more like intake: rooftop landing, sterile elevator, debriefing level, mirrored glass, officers too busy to stare for long but trained enough to know something valuable had arrived. The command officer praised the data dump as comprehensive. Analysts would study it for months. Years of field research had been saved by one machine and one under-briefed operator.

The Agent asked the only reward question that mattered to him: outside communication privileges. The officer hesitated, calculated, and granted them. One Legion-issued secure device. One hour per month. External calls allowed. Monitored by the duty officer and the authorizing command. Revocable on conduct. The [[prop:prop_gamma_comms_privilege|authorization]] is painfully precise because the Legion is most comfortable when kindness has a limit, a supervisor, and a clause.

The Agent accepted. Of course he accepted. The file notes his stated reason: he could finally contact his parents. The line should not be mocked. A monitored hour is still a voice crossing distance. It is also a leash made of minutes. The officer softened when family entered the conversation, and that softness was probably real. Institutions are cruelest when real people inside them can still feel sympathy but can only express it through forms.

This is why the communication device matters enough to file. It is not a shop item. It is not loot. It is a privilege granted because the machine delivered intelligence. The reward ties the Agent's private longing to the Legion's public appetite. Waluigi has seen worse bargains, but few that fit so neatly in one hand.
sections.waluigi_note: The Legion has discovered the smallest possible unit of mercy: sixty minutes, supervised.

sections.name: Mihawk's Debrief and the Problem of Being Nearby
sections.overview:
Mihawk's separation was inevitable. The soldiers had promised no detainment unless necessary, which is one of those sentences that sounds reassuring until one remembers who decides necessity. He was not Legion. He had seen the Underground, the transport, the machine, the extraction, and enough classified behavior to make a cautious institution itch. So he was placed in a secondary chamber, not a cell, and questioned by an officer whose politeness did not make the room less official.

The questions narrowed around role. How had he become involved? What was his connection to the data collector? Did he know what was being gathered? Did he assist in gathering ecological data, battle logs, conversations from monsters? Mihawk answered with the precision of a blade put back in its sheath. He did not collect the data. He was there to ensure safety. His role was protective, not analytical. The [[prop:prop_mihawk_debrief_summary|debrief summary]] accepts that statement and still marks him as exposed.

The lobby scene after the interview is quieter and in some ways more important. Mihawk and the Agent sit near the end of the mission and speak like men who understand that shared danger does not guarantee shared road. The Agent jokes that it truly was an under tale. Mihawk says they made it out with intel that changes things. He asks about the Agent's parents, then realizes the Agent had not told him that. It is a small misstep, but in a file about surveillance and inference, small missteps ring loudly.

Then Mihawk speaks of an unnamed island: isolated, fertile, peaceful, with lions and no formal claim. He had left young to become a pirate. He calls the sea freedom. The officer's later questions about his arrival at Mount Ebott meet only Mihawk's difficult answer: not planned, not coincidence, perhaps fate. To the Legion, this does not clear him. It makes him harder to categorize. A man without a named homeland who walked into a classified mountain and walked out beside a Gamma Agent is exactly the sort of person bureaucracy calls free while assigning someone to watch him.
sections.waluigi_note: The Legion believes a man can be free to walk and still worth watching. This is not contradiction to them. It is policy.

sections.name: The Deadman's Stamp Made the Room Smaller
sections.overview:
The embassy debrief became dangerous when the Agent stopped behaving like a rewarded subordinate and began testing the officer's clearance. The trigger was the mission's hidden casualty knowledge: two KIA, the dead authorizer, the orders that should not have been understood by the person in the room. The officer's professional tone cracked when the Agent implied knowledge she had not expected him to possess. She asked how he knew. That was the wrong question to ask a Gamma Agent who had begun measuring the ceiling.

The Agent pressed. If word got out about his true assignment, would that not be problematic? Was the officer even above the clearance level required to understand why Mihawk ended up at Mount Ebott? She summoned security. The Agent smiled, asked who was really in control, snapped his fingers, and used code Alpha Zeta 2, Protocol 6. The guards answered his command. The room's power diagram redrew itself in a second.

Then came the Real Manual. The Agent read from the hidden authority that ordinary officers had been trained to treat as myth: Article 9-4, Directive 6-Alpha, operation outside standard command, Article 13-7 and termination authority under the Deadman's Stamp. The officer collapsed under the realization that the book on the table was not the same law she had been taught. The [[prop:prop_real_gamma_manual_excerpt|extract]] is filed because it changes the genre of the scene. This is no longer a debrief about a mission. It is a demonstration that the Iron Legion contains a second chain of command with rules sharper than the visible one.

Jamesly's entrance prevents the scene from becoming only terror. He has enough authority to stop the Agent and enough familiarity to sound tired rather than surprised. He calls the Agent a loose cannon, an exceptional asset, and a complication. He names the actual violation: unauthorized interrogation of a civilian operative, execution protocols invoked without clearance. His intervention proves Gamma power has limits, but only limits enforced by people even deeper inside Gamma power.
sections.waluigi_note: When the secret manual is more important than the public manual, the public manual is a costume.

sections.name: The Officer Learned the Manual Was Not the Law
sections.overview:
The unnamed embassy officer begins the scene with ordinary authority. She has a desk, a pen, security within reach and a file she believes contains the relevant facts. That confidence does not survive contact with the Real Manual. The Agent's questions are not random intimidation; they are tests of what the officer knows, what she thinks she knows, and what her institution decided she did not deserve to know. The moment she recognizes the Deadman's Stamp, she changes from interviewer to evidence.

This is a cruel scene, and Waluigi will not pretend otherwise. The Agent pushes too hard. The guards are turned by code. The officer is frightened in a way that goes beyond professional discomfort. But the scene also reveals something the polite version would have hidden: the Legion trains some of its own people to believe the sharpest part of Gamma authority is a myth. When the Agent reads Article 13-7 aloud, the officer is not merely scared of the Agent. She is scared because the floor under her career opens and shows another floor beneath it, one she was never briefed on.

Jamesly calls the Agent reckless for good reason. He also arrives because the room has uncovered a real structural problem. The Legion's visible chain of command cannot supervise what it is not allowed to understand. That is why the officer matters even without a stable name. She is not a villain to defeat. She is the face of the institution discovering, too late, that it has been compartmentalized below the weapon it serves.
sections.waluigi_note: Fear is not proof. But when the trained officer panics at a clause she was told was myth, the panic becomes a filing.

sections.name: Protocol 4871 Made the Room Use Its Real Names
sections.overview:
Jamesly moves the problem into a darker room, and Daniel tries to make it a discipline hearing. The accusation is tidy: unauthorized interrogation, civilian operative, execution protocols, reckless behavior. The Agent does not deny the mess. He asks for procedure before defense: unsterilized names and a Gamma Observer under Protocol 4871.

This is one of the most important small moves in the log. Unsterilized names are not flavor. Sterilized names let institutions discuss people as categories until responsibility becomes fog. A Gamma Observer is not comfort. It is a witness the room cannot easily edit afterward. The Agent has just abused authority in one room and then uses authority correctly in the next to force the debrief to become auditable. Waluigi hates that both things are true, because clean moral sorting is easier to file and less accurate.

Daniel grants the request because protocol still binds him. That matters too. Gamma power is not pure chaos; it has rites, forms, countersignatures, observers, and vocabulary. The hidden state inside the state is still bureaucratic. It simply keeps a more dangerous set of forms. When the Agent names the Deadman's Stamp as a leak concern, Daniel's posture changes because the room now has the right names in it. The charge is no longer only that the Agent threatened someone. It is that someone outside the correct circle knew the threat existed.
sections.waluigi_note: A room that refuses real names is preparing to lie. A room forced to use them has at least been made to sweat honestly.

sections.name: The Breach High Command Would Not Let the Archive Hear
sections.overview:
High Command's chamber is not described for long because the chamber refuses to remain in the record. That refusal is itself a description. Three hooded figures, a circular room, the Agent walking quietly, a familiar voice thanking him for making the journey on short notice, and then the stated problem: an intelligence-network breach. A high-ranking Legion officer has been leaking classified information to an external party. Foreign operatives may be involved.

That is the kind of sentence the whole Mount Ebott survey has been walking toward without knowing it. The survey began as a descent into a hidden civilization, but the final threat is upward and inward: classified information leaving the Legion through someone with rank. Monsterkind's secrecy, the machine's over-recording, the Deadman's Stamp, Mihawk's exposure and the High Command summons are suddenly not separate loose threads. They are examples of the same disease: knowledge moving through channels that the visible authorities cannot fully control.

Then the Agent asks whether he should turn off his logger. High Command says yes. This is not merely operational caution. It is the first confirmed act by the people who claim to investigate the breach, and the act is to create another unlogged space. Waluigi will not claim that proves guilt. Waluigi will claim it proves method. High Command responds to a leak by making a room the archive cannot audit. Perhaps that is necessary. Perhaps it is incriminating. The only honest filing is to mark the moment the record goes dark and refuse to let darkness masquerade as nothing.
sections.waluigi_note: When the people investigating a leak begin by cutting the recorder, Waluigi writes down the scissors.

sections.name: The Summons and the Cutoff
sections.overview:
Jamesly moves the Agent into a higher room, and Daniel begins with discipline. The Agent asks for two procedural protections before the debrief: unsterilized names and a Gamma Observer under Protocol 4871. Daniel grants both, irritated but bound by the rules he still recognizes. That request matters. The Agent may be reckless, but he knows when to make the room use its real nouns. In a file where hidden manuals and false briefings are everywhere, unsterilized names are not courtesy. They are ammunition.

Daniel's accusation is simple: unauthorized interrogation, reckless conduct, protocol breach. The Agent answers with the Deadman's Stamp. The room changes again. If a civilian embassy operative knows that protocol, the issue is no longer only the Agent's conduct. It is leakage. Daniel asks how deep it goes. The Agent raises Mihawk as a factor: a pirate, a witness, someone who thinks the Agent inexperienced but has enough wit to be dangerous. Daniel orders surveillance. The investigation has now grown teeth on both sides: a possible internal leak and an external witness who cannot be allowed to drift unobserved.

A courier interrupts before the debrief can resolve. The [[prop:prop_high_command_summons|summons]] is direct: High Command wants the Agent in person. No video call. No substitute. No delay. The helicopter should have taken days and crossed borders; instead it arrives at the High Command spire almost immediately. The pilot knows the Agent's real name, James, and says they met during training. Geography folds. Procedure narrows.

At the top of the spire, three hooded figures wait. They announce an intelligence-network breach: a high-ranking Legion officer leaking classified information to an external party. The Agent asks whether to turn off his logger. They say yes. The last recorded seconds, preserved in [[prop:prop_final_logger_cutoff|the cutoff slip]], do not reveal the breach. They reveal the method by which the archive was denied the breach. That is enough. The final fact of Mount Ebott is not what High Command said next. It is that High Command knew there was a recorder and chose silence.
sections.waluigi_note: The final fact in the Mount Ebott survey is not what High Command said. It is that High Command knew where the recorder was and turned it off.

aftermath:
## Immediate Position

The Mount Ebott survey team has left the Underground. That is the cleanest success in the file and the least complicated sentence anyone gets to keep. Mihawk and the Gamma Agent reached the surface alive. The transport did not require destroying the Barrier. Asgore and Toriel's egress condition was accepted. Wing Gaster's machine worked. Koffin-K's emergency did not stop the second transport.

Everything after that complicates the success.

## Custody

The recovered survey machine and data packet are in Iron Legion custody at the Old World Embassy. The handover receipt states that the device contains not only ecological readings but conversations, battle readings, energy levels and monster-technology scans. The Gamma Agent did not know the machine had that scope when he carried it through the Underground. This does not remove responsibility from the Legion. It relocates it from field behavior to equipment design and briefing.

The Gamma Agent retains a Legion-issued monitored communication device under a one-hour-per-month allowance. This is a real privilege and a real control mechanism. Both are filed.

Mihawk is not detained in the immediate record. He cooperated with debriefing and maintained that he served as protective support rather than data collector. Daniel's later surveillance order means he is not free in the way ordinary civilians use that word. He is free in the Legion sense: not in a cell, but in a file.

## Personnel and Standing

Jamesly has entered the active Gamma file as a senior handler able to interrupt the Agent. Daniel has entered as a command debrief authority who began with discipline and pivoted to breach review when the Deadman's Stamp became evidence of a leak. The unnamed embassy officer remains unpromoted to a character record because the log does not give a stable name and because her importance is procedural: she is the person whose knowledge reveals the leak risk.

## Open Threats

Koffin-K's emergency remains unknown. The Deadman's Stamp leak remains unresolved. Mihawk is a monitored witness. High Command's intelligence-network breach is established but not described because the logger was disabled at the threshold of the briefing. The missing minutes are not a gap in the archive's attention. They are an imposed silence.

## RNN and Follow-Up

The event has been added to the RNN pending list. No broadcast is cut from this single filing alone. The investigation file **The Oath, the Machine, and the Missing Minutes** now carries the evidence trail and should be the next place a reader goes if they want to argue with the silence.

## Emotional Carry-Forward

The Agent leaves this log with more authority than comfort. He has a phone privilege, but it is watched. He has High Command's attention, but not its trust. He has completed the survey, but the machine's hidden scope means success may have violated the spirit of the oath he just watched others swear. Mihawk leaves with less certainty than his composure suggests: no named homeland, no clear next port, and now a surveillance shadow because he stood close to the truth and did not flinch.

Waluigi's true discomfort is this: everyone in the final log is both helped and used. The Underground helps the visitors leave while using their silence. The Legion rewards the Agent while using his longing. The Agent frightens the officer while using her fear to test a leak. Jamesly saves the officer while using forgetfulness as cleanup. High Command calls the Agent while using darkness as a wall. This is not a clean victory. It is a successful extraction from one underground into another.
waluigiAssessment:
## Waluigi's Assessment

**The oath and the machine contradict each other.** Asgore and Toriel required silence because monsterkind's survival depends on remaining myth to the surface. That is understandable. Waluigi, who enjoys gossip, still understands why a hidden civilization does not want to become the subject of a bored empire's field study. But the survey machine had already made myth into data. The Agent's mouth could keep the oath. The machine's memory could not. This is why equipment design is diplomacy whether soldiers admit it or not.

**Wing Gaster's transport is cleaner than the institutions around it.** The Gaster Blaster looks like a weapon and behaves like a door. Disturbing? Yes. Efficient? Also yes. The science itself is almost honest compared to the politics that follow. It sends Mihawk and the Agent to the surface inside the same world's plane. It does not pretend to be a flower, a treaty, a phone call or a mercy. It does the one thing it says it will do. WAH! Waluigi did not expect to compliment the skull cannon.

**Koffin-K's interruption must not be thrown away.** A theatrical man arrived without theatrics and said there was an emergency. Then the transport took the Agent before the sentence could finish. That is not a joke. It is an uncollected debt. The next Ebott-adjacent filing should recover what Koffin-K meant or explicitly state that the warning was lost. An unexplained emergency is not flavor. It is a loaded shelf in a dark room.

**The communication privilege is both reward and leash.** One hour a month to call outside is meaningful. Waluigi will not sneer at a person wanting to contact family. But the conditions matter: monitored, revocable, justified by intelligence value. The Legion has turned longing into a compliance instrument. This is the sort of cruelty that smiles because it has technically helped.

**Mihawk is innocent of the wrong charge.** He did not gather data. He said so, and the record gives no reason to call that false. But the Legion is not only worried about guilt. It is worried about exposure. Mihawk saw the mission, the machine, the embassy, and enough of Gamma procedure to become dangerous by memory alone. His reward for honesty is surveillance consideration. Again: that is not contradiction in Legion logic. It is the point.

**The Real Manual is an empire inside the empire.** The Deadman's Stamp, Directive 6-Alpha, and Protocol 4871 reveal a hidden operating constitution. Public command still exists, but Gamma authority can step behind it, around it, and sometimes through it. The embassy officer's fear matters because she had been trained to treat part of the law as myth. When a state lies to its own officers about what its agents may do, the state is no longer keeping secrets from enemies. It is keeping secrets from its own hands.

**Final verdict:** the Mount Ebott Survey did not end when the team reached the surface. It ended when High Command turned off the logger. That is the moment the archive finally meets a wall built specifically for it. The file's last fact is therefore not the content of the breach briefing; the content is missing. The last fact is authorship of the silence. Someone with authority knew the logger existed, disabled it, and continued speaking. Waluigi cannot file what came next. Waluigi can file who made sure he could not.
